utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please be seated. Can the registrar please call the case number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Case number IT-95-10-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. Good afternoon to everybody. We will have the appearances in a few seconds, but can the accused please be brought in first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please sit down, Mr. Jelisic. I will ask you to give us your full identity in a few moments for the transcript, but first of all, I would like to have the appearances. Mr. Jelisic, once again, you may be seated. In a few minutes, I will ask you to stand up again, but first we will have the appearances. For the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Terree Bowers. My colleagues are Vladimir Tochilovsky. Also joining us is Geoffrey Nice, who will be replacing me on my departure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Are you about to leave us, Mr. Bowers? You've only just started on this trial. That's not very nice of you. Thank you very much anyway. For the Defence, please, can we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Veselin Londrovic, attorney from Bijeljina, and on the team for the accused Jelisic are Mr. Greaves, attorney from Great Britain, and Attorney Babic from Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. Mr. Greaves, can you spell out your name for me, and can you introduce yourself fully? Your name is Greaves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Michael Greaves, G-R-E-A-V-E-S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm from the bar of England and Wales; we making a small distinction between our Scottish neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Well, we will not enter the details of this nationality or that nationality. We could enter a very difficult debate. You are from the bar of England. That's sufficient. Mr. Jelisic, I now turn towards you. Could you please give us your full name, your age, your date of birth, and could you tell us where you worked before you were arrested and where you lived before being arrested? Mr. Jelisic, could you please stand and answer these questions I've just put to you? Can you hear me, Mr. Jelisic, in a language you understand? It seems there's a technical problem. Mr. Jelisic is not getting any interpretation. All right, fine. Mr. Jelisic, since you can now hear me, please stand up, and please state clearly your full name, the date and place of your birth, and tell us where you worked before your arrest and where you lived before your arrest.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm Goran Jelisic from Bijeljina. I was born on 7 June, 1968, in Bijeljina. Before the arrest, I worked at the agricultural combine, Sembrija near Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) And you lived in Bijeljina, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. You may now be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) For the public's sake, I'm just specifying that it's not customary for the Judges of this Tribunal to come in so late, but we had to discuss a very important issue before declaring this particular trial open. We will now get started. Mr. Bowers, I think you are about to make an opening statement; is that what you had planned to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I am prepared to make an opening statement. We have a few items, such as our request for protective orders. I don't know if the Court wants to take that as a preliminary matter or wait until after the opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No. First of all, first of all, Mr. Bowers, I wanted to know whether or not you would be giving your opening statement today pursuant to Article 84 of the Rules -- Rule 84. For the public's sake, the public being present today, as is customary, for the public's sake then, I would like to specify that on November 25th, the Judges of this Tribunal have been assigned this case. On my left is Judge Riad, on my right is Judge Rodrigues. I am Judge Jorda; I am Presiding Judge for this case. So on November 25th, we have tried to give an answer to an issue raised by the Defence counsel; i.e., was the accused able to follow the hearings during his trial? We have asked for a commission of medical experts to study Mr. Jelisic's case and to tell us whether or not he was able to follow the hearings. I will ask the legal officer of the Chamber to give us the conclusions of Dr. Duits and Dr. van der Veen. Please read out the conclusions of this report, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Three questions had been put to the accused. The first question: "Is the accused suffering from a mental illness, and if so, which?" The answer to that question has been the following: "The subject does not have a mental illness. He does have a serious personality disorder in the sense that he suffers from a borderline personality disorder with anti-social and narcissistic tendencies which have probably existed since adolescence. These tendencies have possibly been superimposed on an earlier behavioural disorder."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Registrar, could you please read out the last conclusion? I don't wish to enter into too much details. These details should not be made public. The Defence raised a number of legitimate issues, and I would like the Defence to be fully convinced of the fact that the accused is fit to stand trial. So please read the third conclusion of the medical report, and please give us the answer to the question that states: "Is the accused fit to stand trial, scheduled to start 30th November, 1998, which will last for three days and resume in January 1999?" I will ask you to give us the answer to that question only. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The answer to the question is, "Yes, the subject is fit to stand trial."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) So it is on the basis of these conclusions that Mr. Jelisic is here today. Mr. Londrovic, I think this answers your questions. I see that you are raising your hand. Just a minute. I would like to state that Mr. Londrovic gave the Judges full leeway to decide whether or not Mr. Jelisic should be examined by a commission of psychological experts or not. Yes, Mr. Londrovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I would just like to request to go into closed session for a brief period in order for the Defence to be able to address some procedural issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am turning to my colleagues. Would you rather bring these issues up before the Prosecutor's opening statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) How long do you need, Mr. Londrovic? Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's a matter I'm going to raise with Your Honours. It will take, I think, about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well then. We'll just go into private session, and after hearing your arguments, Mr. Greaves, we will go back into open session and we will then hear the Prosecutor's opening statement. Mr. Registrar, could you please make sure that we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, I was dealing, I hope, as quickly as possible, with Article 21. Your Honours will recall that Article 21(4) sets out a number of what are described as minimum guarantees to an accused. There are three which are relevant: Article 21(4)(B), which sets out that he has adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and communicate with counsel of his own choosing; Article 21(4)(C), which guarantees him to be tried without undue delay; and Article 21(4)(F), to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in the International Tribunal. 21(4)(B) is relevant to the present matter in that it guarantees his right to communicate with counsel of his choice. As well as having leading counsel, he has chosen me to act as his co-counsel, but we have not, as yet, had a satisfactory opportunity to communicate concerning his defence. The result of that is that I, for my part, if called upon to cross-examine the witnesses, would have to say that I did not feel that I was in a proper position so to do and that I did not feel that I was adequately prepared to cross-examine the witnesses. The third matter is this: There has been prepared for submission to the Tribunal a document which sets out three special defences. It has not yet been filed. Those three defences are: alibi, in relation to incidents which took place after the 19th of May, 1992; secondly, diminished responsibility; and thirdly, duress. That document was prepared recently. I, for one, have not yet had an opportunity of considering it at length, and certainly have not gone into the documents which are set out in that notice, and, for example, Your Honours have referred to the medical report, the conclusion of which was read out in public. That document is in Dutch and hasn't yet been translated into English or French, as I understand it, and is unlikely to be so until Wednesday. Whilst that report touches on the issue of fitness to stand trial, it may well contain matters which are relevant to any issue of diminished responsibility which is raised. Plainly, the issue of his mental health and some of the features that were read out at the beginning of the Registry's presentation of that matter might affect the question of whether he had the requisite mens rea. Can I make it perfectly plain, Your Honour, that we make this application very conscious of the fact that there are witnesses here in The Hague who are ready to testify before Your Honours and that any adjournment of their participation in the trial is, of course, unfortunate and to be regretted. And I'm anxious that Your Honours should be aware that we are very much alive to the problems that the Victims and Witnesses Unit have over witnesses who get brought here but do not give evidence as arranged, but we make the application nevertheless. Our first submission is this: That given the circumstances that prevail, it would be proper to give effect to the guarantees set out in Article 21 to enable the whole of the Defence team, which the defendant has chosen to act for him, to be fully and adequately prepared. This is a most grave charge, and he faces the very real possibility of a life sentence of imprisonment. It's important that he has the opportunity to know that his counsel are fully prepared and communicate fully with them. I accept, of course, there would be a delay involved in the process I have outlined to Your Honour, but the only prejudice to the Prosecution would be, in my submission, that they had brought witnesses here who had unfortunately to return to their native countries. As far as court time is concerned, there would be only a minimal amount of time lost. I would also hope, and I hope Your Honours will bear this closely in mind, although I cannot promise it, some delay might enable us further to restrict and define the issues which are to be tried by Your Honours. I've spoke briefly to two of my learned friends for the Prosecution this morning and indicated to them that I would, of course, be open to further discussions if we can limit, in any way, some of the issues that you have to try, if at all possible. Obviously, I haven't had the chance to do that as yet. In all those circumstances, we invite you to accede to the request for an adjournment. If Your Honours don't accept --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You didn't talk about the essential point. What would be the date you would propose because I suppose you would need a long preparation, so do you have any idea of the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I deal with two final suggestions that I have? If you are against me on the general proposition that I've just made, I have two alternative suggestions. The first is this: If you wish to commence the trial, you should hear only the Prosecution's opening address and then adjourn so that it may properly be said that we have started on time and at least have done some work today and possibly tomorrow morning, although I don't know how long my learned friend is going to be in his opening address. The second alternative, and I know this because I have spoken this morning with Mr. Bowers, I know that this is one which doesn't appeal to the Prosecution, but I proffer it to Your Honours for your consideration, is that you could commence the trial by hearing the Prosecution's opening address and then having witnesses called but only giving their examination-in-chief and not at that stage being cross-examined. I can understand the reluctance of the Prosecution, but I put that forward as an alternative suggestion. Your Honour, I know that you are always concerned about the rights of the defendant to have a speedy trial, and that's one matter that I considered when asking you to balance his various rights under Article 21. We have discussed this at length with the accused. He has been asked his views about the delay, and he has signed a notice declaring that he is content with the course that we have adopted, and I have a copy available for Your Honours to see if you would wish. So the matter has been canvassed with him, and he is content that we make this application today. As to Your Honour's point that you raised, I heard the date of, I think, January 1999. Your Honour, I would hope to be well in order by the New Year from a personal point of view. I hope that I've said all that I can. Is there any other matter on which I can assist any of Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No from the Registry. We are going to ask the Prosecution for their opinion, but I haven't quite understood. You wish us to delay the proceedings for the benefit of Mr. Jelisic or yourself because as far as I have been able to follow so far, it is for your own benefit because you were not here at the beginning, you arrived today, you did not attend the Pre-Trial conference that was held -- when was it, Mr. Fourmy -- the 18th of November. Therefore, I heard some very pertinent arguments. I also heard reference to the right of the accused to a speedy trial. And today you have behind you the experience of the Celebici trial, but I must say that the arguments were primarily to allow you to converse with the accused who speaks Serbo-Croatian. You told us that you can speak Serbo-Croatian only well enough to order a beer. I don't know whether you will have a greater knowledge of the language by the beginning of January. We in this case have the opposite problem. Usually, we have attorneys who only speak Serbo-Croatian, but in this case, it's a different case, a different matter. As I said, I don't know whether by January you will speak Serbo-Croatian sufficiently to be able to converse with the accused. The agreement of the accused -- Mr. Jelisic has been asked for his opinion every time. We heard him last time criticise Mr. Kostic. Mr. Greaves, at the end of January when you will be ready and, perhaps, Mr. Jelisic or yourself or Mr. Londrovic requests the presence of a fourth counsel who may be of a completely different nationality, would we again be in a position to have to postpone? I think that the right of the accused is taken very seriously by you, that is your mission, but equally by the Judges. They too have a very lofty mission. I should like first to hear the Prosecution and then your colleagues from the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have been in this situation or a similar situation several times in this case. Goran Jelisic's first Defence counsel, who was Mr. Pantelic, was withdrawn from this case in April of this year on the request of the accused. In August '98, another counsel, Mr. Kostic, was assigned as co-counsel for Mr. Jelisic. Soon after that assignment, Mr. Kostic requested for a continuance of the trial date. In November '98, again at the request of the accused, Mr. Kostic was withdrawn from the case, and now another co-counsel, Mr. Greaves, is assigned to assist Mr. Londrovic, and again the same request for an adjournment of the proceedings. The fact is that it is still Mr. Londrovic who is the lead Defence counsel for Mr. Jelisic, and Mr. Greaves is only to assist him. Mr. Londrovic has been the leading counsel for the accused from April 1998. Since then, he has had more than six months to read witness statements, to prepare cross-examinations, to prepare the Defence case. Therefore, the Prosecution doesn't see any violation of Article 21 of the ICTY Statute, and, therefore, we object to any adjournment of the hearing. With regard to preparation for cross-examination by one of the co-counsel who is Mr. Greaves, the Defence can start cross-examination of the Prosecution's first witness today and continue it tomorrow morning. Therefore, tonight, for such an experienced lawyer as Mr. Greaves is, the Defence will have sufficient time and opportunity to prepare for the cross-examination of both the first witness and the second witness who will testify -- the second witness who will testify either today or tomorrow. All in all, the Prosecution doesn't see any violation of Article 21, and we will insist that there should be no adjournment granted to the Defence, and the trial should commence today. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Before deliberating, I should like to hear the opinion of Mr. Londrovic, Mr. Babic, and then Mr. Jelisic. Mr. Londrovic, what do you feel? You have been the lead counsel of the accused for many months. You didn't tell us at the 18th of November Status Conference that you had any difficulties or that you were going to resort to another attorney. On the contrary, when I asked Mr. Jelisic, you confirmed that Mr. Kostic was no longer the third counsel of the accused, and today we see a new co-counsel. Can you give some explanations to the Judges? We would like to hear those explanations. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, on the 18th of November, the Pre-Trial conference, the accused, Goran Jelisic, informed you that his co-Defence counsel would no longer be Mr. Nikola Kostic. He's an attorney from the United States. He has fallen ill. He is suffering from pneumonia and diabetes, so that he was unable to carry out his duties according to the Defence plan. Mr. Jelisic, therefore, withdrew his assignment to Mr. Kostic, even though it is not something that he should do, but I, upon Goran Jelisic's insistence, agreed with him and informed the Registry accordingly. My personal opinion and that of Mr. Babic is that in such a serious trial, I would even refer to it as a historic trial, as this is the first time that the charge is genocide, myself and Mr. Babic, coming from a civil law system, need the assistance of a respected attorney from the other system, and we opted for Mr. Greaves, who is very knowledgable about the common law system. I can understand the Trial Chamber, that they may be irritated by all of this, and I understand also the Prosecution, but I hope that the Court will show trust and believe us if we say that we will not ask for any adjournment again. So I appeal to you on behalf of the whole Defence team that we adjourn the proceedings, and I hope that there will be no further changes or, rather, I can guarantee that there will be no further changes in the Defence team and that the trial can begin in January. We have been told that this trial should resume between the 25th and the 29th. The Court would not lose much time, and I think that the Defence, in view of the seriousness of the charges, that is, the charge of genocide, would be far better prepared then than if the trial were to begin today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Babic, do you have anything to say? I'm asking you the same question I addressed to Mr. Londrovic. I have the same question for you as for Mr. Londrovic. I didn't understand at the previous meeting that you were going to appeal to a new co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I really have nothing more to add to what Mr. Londrovic has said, so if you could accept what he said as the position of the Defence as a whole. Indeed, for Mr. Londrovic and myself, we are faced with very serious problems in organising the defence properly and the beginning of trial in accordance with the Rules and Statute and its provisions. We really do hope that we have by now resolved all the problems related to the Defence team and the composition of that team and that, in the very near future, we could begin the trial properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Before the Judges deliberate at the bench, Mr. Jelisic, can you stand up, please? The last time we saw each other at the Pre-Trial conference, we examined the outlines of the trial, and as far as your Defence counsel was concerned, it was clear that you no longer wanted to have one of the Defence counsel, that is, Mr. Kostic, and that you had trust in Mr. Londrovic and in Mr. Babic. What is your viewpoint at this stage? Will you please express your views about this matter before the Judges deliberate? Are there any specific problems that you had with these two attorneys that you had to appeal to a third? What is your opinion? Will you please present it to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, in the last few days, some unexpected problems arose in connection with my defence, and all I would have to say would be to support the position of my attorneys in the interest of the best possible defence which is, of course, in my interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. The Judges are going to deliberate at the bench. Mr. Greaves, Mr. Londrovic, Mr. Babic, the Defence team, Mr. Tochilovsky, who responded: The Judges decided, taking the following into consideration: First of all, they feel that there have already been many changes on the Defence side since the beginning and the arrest of Mr. Jelisic and since his arrival in The Hague. Secondly, that Mr. Jelisic has had two Defence counsel throughout who speak the language of the accused, that is, Mr. Londrovic as the lead counsel and Mr. Babic as his co-counsel, who are perfectly familiar with the language. Regarding Mr. Greaves, the Judges note that there is no judicial system that would envisage such things, but there are, in some rules and regulations, characteristics of a particular system which one or another lawyer may be more familiar with, but the rules and regulations give preponderance to the initiative that the Judges have to take. Fourthly, Article 73 bis of a recent date envisaged a Pre-Trial Conference which closes the preliminary stage of the investigations and, in a sense, sets the outline of the proceedings. It is in that context that 73 bis, paragraph (F) allows, if the Trial Chamber wishes, to file, seven days prior to the date set for trial, a list of factual and legal issues as well as a Pre-Trial brief. Also, the Chamber feels, regarding the defence of alibi, this should be submitted prior to the beginning of trial, and this hasn't been done by the Defence. Fifth, at a factual level, before going back to the principles, that, unfortunately, for various reasons and independent of the will of the Judges, the trial will take place for three days, beginning today, but will have to be interrupted until the end of January, which again will give time for the Defence, if necessary - Mr. Greaves in this case - all the time necessary to familiarise himself not only with -- not the common law system but the law of the Tribunal and the facts of the case and also to converse with Jelisic, not only through the intermediary of the two attorneys but also an interpreter which the registry will certainly place at the disposal of the accused in the detention facility. Sixth, the Judges take into account the rights of the accused and also the superior interests of international justice. The rights of the accused have not been prejudiced in any sense. At our last Status Conference, the wish was expressed to have the most expeditious possible trial. The very text of the Statute requires of the Judges, according to very high international standards, that the trial be fair and expeditious and that the expeditiousness should not affect fairness, and as regards fairness, I think the accused benefits from a Defence counsel which has been very well composed from the very beginning of the proceedings. As for the interests of justice, the understanding of the Judges is that they should defend public order, and it is not legal assistance where the Prosecution is opposed to the Defence with the Judges as neutral arbiters, and I ask the Defence to read in detail the regulations, the very great importance the Judges attach to the establishment of the truth. Finally, and perhaps most important of all, the interests of the victims and witnesses. The witnesses who know that they need to appear here for three days and then again in January, and any further delay in the proceedings can only prolong the time required for protection. In order to comfort Mr. Greaves, it is not a question of sacrificing, in any sense, the rights of the accused. If this should appear necessary, the possibility will be taken into account of envisaging certain additional time. The examination-in-chief will be done by the Prosecution now and the Defence tomorrow, but the Judges will certainly be responsive to any request in that sense. Therefore, our ruling is that the trial will begin after a ten-minute break with the opening statement of the Prosecution. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please be seated. I would like the accused to be brought in after the Judges arrive in the courtroom, please, Mr. Registrar. It is not appropriate for the accused to wait for the Judges. It is not the procedure we usually use. The Judges come in the courtroom and then enters the accused. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor so that we can have your opening statement in accordance or pursuant with Rule 84. Mr. Bowers, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court: Before the fighting started in Brcko, it was a prosperous and peaceful place. The city is located on the Sava River which divides Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and has a port facility known as Luka. Luka is a large complex. As you enter through the main gate, there are offices on the right and large hangars or warehouses on the left. The city of Brcko, like Bosnia and Herzegovina itself, was ethnically mixed with Bosnian Muslims, Serbs, and Croats living together. According to the 1991 census, the Bosnian Muslims constituted about 45 per cent of the population. Now very few Muslims live there at all. At approximately 5.30 in the morning of the 30th of April, 1992, the peace of Brcko was shattered by two consecutive explosions on the bridges that spanned the Sava River. The first explosion killed numerous pedestrians who were on the bridge when the bomb detonated. Body parts landed throughout the central portion of the city. The explosions served as the signal for the Bosnian Serb attack and takeover of the city. Brcko was a critical target for the Bosnian Serbs because the city sits right in the middle of the so-called Posavina corridor which connects the western Krajina section of Bosnia with the northeastern and eastern sections in which the Bosnian Serbs reside. The Posavina corridor served as a critical bottleneck between the two geographical areas controlled by the Bosnian Serbs. Because Brcko was so important, the Bosnian Serbs unleashed a violent campaign of ethnic cleansing in the municipality. JNA artillery units shelled the city, while local militia, paramilitary units from other areas of Bosnia and Serbia, and other volunteers united in a destructive wave to cleanse the area of non-Serbs. The accused Goran Jelisic was one of the individuals sent to Brcko to assist in the ethnic cleansing. Before the war, Goran Jelisic had been an agricultural machinery mechanic from Bijeljina, a city which is located slightly southeast of Brcko. Earlier in 1992, a local court had sentenced Goran Jelisic to serve three years in prison for a conviction on fraud. Bosnian Serb authorities, however, had more expansive plans for Jelisic, and within a short period of time, Goran Jelisic found himself in a police uniform in the middle of Brcko. His presence in Brcko in 1992 was the result of a Bosnian Serb strategy to unlock the jailhouse doors in order to provide sufficient executioners for the genocidal and ethnic cleansing activities which took place in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If counsel could slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: We are not certain of the exact date on which Goran Jelisic arrived in Brcko, but from eyewitnesses, we know that by the first week in May 1992, Goran Jelisic was executing prisoners outside of the police station in downtown Brcko. A photograph of one of those executions made it into international newspapers. The Prosecution intends to introduce that particular newspaper photograph into evidence. It is quite dramatic evidence of what Goran Jelisic was up to in those early days in Brcko. Jelisic has admitted that he is the policeman depicted in the photograph and that he carried out that particular execution. But as the Court knows from Goran Jelisic's guilty please, Jelisic killed additional detainees outside of the police station. In addition to executing detainees at the police station, Goran Jelisic moved to the Luka warehouse facilities on the Sava River where hundreds of Bosnian Muslim and some Bosnian Croat men were being detained. For approximately two weeks, Goran Jelisic acted as the chief executioner at Luka camp. He held the power of life and death in his hands, and systematically and regularly went about killing the Muslim detainees as well as several Croats. His trademarks were a blue police shirt, a pistol, and a preference for executing detainees over a metal drainage grate. This particular trial will be more focused than the average trial because the accused has already admitted to twelve murders charged in the indictment. The Defence and the Prosecution jointly submitted a factual basis for the entry of the guilty pleas. Investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor have extensively interviewed Goran Jelisic, and he does not deny that he committed multiple murders in the Luka complex. In the interviews, Goran Jelisic has even admitted to committing murders that were not charged in the indictment. During this trial, we will introduce some of the more revealing statements which Goran Jelisic made to investigators. Because of the prior admissions and the entry of the guilty pleas, the Prosecution's case in chief will concentrate on proving that Goran Jelisic committed the murders in Brcko with a genocidal intent. As the Court knows, in order to convict Goran Jelisic of genocide, the Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Goran Jelisic committed the murders at the police station and at the Luka camp with the intent to destroy in whole or in part a racial, ethnical, or religious group. For purposes of this indictment, the Prosecutor has charged that Goran Jelisic committed his murders with the intent to destroy a part of the Bosnian Muslim population. It is important to emphasise at the outset that under the law, Goran Jelisic could be guilty of genocide if he had committed a single murder with the intent to destroy a racial, ethnical, or religious group. In this trial, however, we will establish that Goran Jelisic killed a high number of people during his genocidal spree in Brcko. We will never be able to fix the exact number. If he would be pressed to fix the number, he could not fix that number himself because of the cavalier nature in which he committed the executions and the great number of executions. But if we are to believe even a small percentage of the totals which Goran Jelisic claimed, then his victims certainly number well over a hundred. Not only is the number of victims substantial for purposes of prosecuting a genocide case, but the Prosecution will also establish that the portion of the group which Goran Jelisic set out to destroy was a significant portion of the Muslim population within the Brcko municipality. We will introduce evidence that shows that Bosnian Serb officials in the municipality drew up lists of those individuals who would be executed, thereby targeting intellectuals, military-aged men, and political leaders. By the end of the evidentiary presentation, you will see that the victim group targeted by Goran Jelisic was both significant in its importance to the Bosnian Muslim community and substantial in number. In criminal cases where the Prosecution must prove the subjective intent of the accused, the Prosecution must often rely, almost exclusively, on circumstantial evidence in order to prove that intent. The case against Goran Jelisic, however, is horrifically unique in that we have numerous witnesses who can testify about what Jelisic said at the time of his executions. A person's words are perhaps the most accurate and edifying indicator of the inner workings of his mind. This Court will be presented with the unique opportunity to listen to and analyse the very words Mr. Jelisic spoke as he carried out his genocidal ambitions. The heart and the strength of the Prosecution's case will be elicited from the victim witnesses who saw and heard Goran Jelisic during his activities in Brcko. Many of these witnesses corroborate each other. Permit me to quickly review some of the anticipated testimony which demonstrates Goran Jelisic's genocidal intent. First, numerous witnesses will testify that Goran Jelisic referred to himself as the Serbian Adolf. He, himself, during his initial appearance before this Tribunal, admitted that he went by the nickname of Adolf. The context in which Goran Jelisic used this nickname will demonstrate conclusively that this was not some form of endearment but was a direct reference to the genocidal activities of Adolf Hitler in World War II. Indeed, one witness describes Goran Jelisic as stating to the effect, "Hitler was the first Adolf. I am the second." It matters little whether others gave Jelisic the nickname or whether he adopted it himself. What the evidence will show is that, regardless of the genesis of the nickname, Goran Jelisic used the nickname with a perverse pride in the genocidal symbolism it represented. In addition to the use of the nickname "Adolf," numerous witnesses will testify that Jelisic openly bragged that the reason he had come to Brcko was to kill Muslims and to kill as many as possible. You will hear from at least one witness who tells of a confrontation which occurred when Goran Jelisic first took control at the Luka detention centre. As Goran Jelisic began harassing detainees, a local Serb from Brcko attempted to intervene. Jelisic became angry and said, in effect, "Do you know who I am," and stated that all he had to do was to make a telephone call to resolve the matter. Goran walked off, came back. According to the testimony from the witnesses, Goran remained in control, and the local Serb was not seen again. Goran Jelisic did not hide the fact that the reason he had come to Brcko was to kill as many Muslims as possible. One witness states that Jelisic bragged he had to kill 20 or 30 Muslims before he had his morning coffee. During his murderous spree, Goran Jelisic kept daily tallies of the number of Muslims he had killed. Numerous witnesses will testify about Goran Jelisic announcing his most recent totals. Goran Jelisic often told the detainees themselves how many Muslims he had killed at given points in time. Jelisic also told the guards in Luka camp how many individuals he had killed. Jelisic often set goals for himself by vowing not to rest until he had killed a certain total of detainees on a certain day. Once Goran Jelisic, according to one of the witnesses you will hear, even declined assistance from a guard with regard to a planned execution, noting that he, Goran Jelisic, was still in good form, even though he had killed over 60 people that day. Some of the daily tallies may have ranged into the high sixties, yet Goran Jelisic continued with his daily carnage. The victim witness testimony will also establish that Goran Jelisic was not a reluctant tool of the genocide who was being compelled by Serb authorities to act against his will. Quite to the contrary, the testimony will firmly establish that Goran Jelisic was an efficient and enthusiastic participant in the genocide. One witness had the unfortunate experience of being with Goran Jelisic when Jelisic executed individuals over the metal grate. As mentioned previously, Goran Jelisic often executed his victims over the grate in order to minimise the amount of clean-up after the execution. The grates fed into a drainage system which led out into the Sava River. This particular witness will testify that he watched as Jelisic forced a detainee to kneel over the grate and then shot him in the head. Jelisic then turned to the witness and said something to the effect of "I can see that you are scared. It is nice to kill people this way. I kill them nicely. I don't feel anything." Goran Jelisic became so effective and so notorious during his genocidal spree that even the Bosnian Serb authorities had to rein him in. You will hear from witnesses that around the 19th or 20th of May, 1992, some Bosnian Serb officials removed Goran Jelisic from Luka detention centre. Earlier in mid-May, however, when Jelisic first heard that an army major wanted to stop his killing, according to a witness, Goran Jelisic responded that he, Goran Jelisic, was the boss and that the Luka detention centre was not within the jurisdiction of the army. Jelisic said that he was ready to have a war with the army if they wanted him to stop his killing. Four or five days later, however, someone was able to get Goran Jelisic removed from the Luka camp. But for this eventual removal of Jelisic, he would have continued killing until he had fully decimated the detainee population. It is also important to note that Goran Jelisic understood how his individual actions fit into the broader genocidal campaign which had been launched by the Bosnian Serb authorities. During interviews with OTP investigators, Jelisic explained that upon his arrival in Brcko, the head of the Serbian crisis staff provided Jelisic with a list of Muslims and instructed Jelisic to kill as many of the Muslims as possible. Through the witness testimony, we will also show that Goran Jelisic was not just a mere guard within the Luka camp but that he exhibited and exercised considerable authority. Particularly during the night, Goran Jelisic had free rein to do whatever he wanted to with the detainees. Often, he ordered guards to assist him in his activities and the guards complied. To the detainees whose lives were held in balance on an hourly basis, Goran Jelisic was the primary, if not the only, authority figure. As one witness put it, "To us, he was like a god. He controlled whether we lived or whether we died." It is appropriate and just that the Prosecution has pursued charges against individuals such as Goran Jelisic because without key executioners in the various geographical areas, the Bosnian Serb authorities would not have been able to implement the ethnic cleansing and genocidal campaign on which they embarked in the spring and summer of 1992. Accordingly, at the conclusion of the evidence, we will request this Court to find Goran Jelisic guilty of genocide because to the victims in Brcko, the face of genocide was the face of Goran Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. Before hearing the Prosecution's case, I think a certain number of principles should be established. You know that the Rules have changed on a number of issues and that the Rules now give the Judges a certain number of powers which may be important, and I'm now turning to Mr. Greaves, which may be more important than in the common law systems. These new powers stem from the first trials in this Tribunal. I would now like to focus your attention, and I'm turning to the Prosecution and the Defence, to Rule 90(G). You will have to keep in mind this Rule when you present your arguments. The Judges have control on the presentation of the arguments of the Prosecution and the Defence so that all the arguments can be presented in an efficient manner and to avoid wasting time. Article 90 says that the cross-examination, and I now turn to the Defence, should be limited itself to the points addressed in the examination-in-chief. In other trials, this Rule has been interpreted in different ways. Of course, people who are familiar with the common law systems are very familiar with this Rule, but sometimes it's not very easy to apply it in this Tribunal. So the Judges have said that this Rule should be applied with a certain flexibility, and if we had to limit only the cross-examination to the examination-in-chief, of course, it would be very easy. The witness would come and testify on a very limited area or very limited events, and the person in charge of the cross-examination would not have the possibility to use the presence of this witness to ask questions about issues that may be of interest to this party. I would like to remind you that the new Rule 73(C) bis allows the Judges to make the cross-examination shorter. Of course, all the witnesses did not go through the same experiences and events. For instance, if you take the example of an UNPROFOR officer, maybe his testimony could be shorter than a person who was raped or went through very difficult ordeals. However, I would like to remind the Prosecution today, but maybe tomorrow the Defence, the Judges have the power to make the cross-examination shorter than the examination-in-chief. Then, of course, Mr. Greaves, I'm sure you will read Rule 98 of the Rules. Maybe this is a power that the Judges have here and that you won't find in the common law systems. The Judges can have the power to bring some new witnesses if they wish to do so or they can obtain additional evidence if they wish to do so, so be aware of all these provisions. The Judges may have the need to intervene during the proceedings. Of course, this is not what we wish to do, but it may be necessary. Now, as far as witnesses are concerned, I'm turning to the Prosecution, when you have a witness in the courtroom, the Judges want the witness to testify on the charges which are in the indictment. So that we don't have to intervene, please make sure that the witness tells his whole story if it is necessary in order to confirm one of the charges in the indictment. Sometimes the witness gets tired. It's always very difficult to come here to The Hague for these witnesses. Sometimes it's very far away from the place they come from, but it's always very difficult as well for a witness to come in front of a Tribunal. Usually, they are not familiar with Tribunals and with legal procedures. Thirdly, the Judges would like you to remain focused on the various elements of the charges. A witness is here to throw some light on various precise points of the indictment. A witness can come to say that his house was on fire. Of course, it can be very important for the witness to address other questions, and if that's the case, please do it, but please always remember your final objective, and I am turning to the Prosecution and to the Defence. For instance, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, you want to prove the facts that constitute the charge of genocide. Here, you are in front of a Tribunal. You are not in front of an investigation committee or not in front of a commission whose job it is to write a report. We are Judges, and, beyond any reasonable doubt, we have to determine if the accused is guilty or innocent. After all these considerations, the Judges, and I'm turning to Mr. Tochilovsky and to Mr. Bowers, the Judges will make sure that the witness can speak freely. Of course, we will adopt this procedure to the different witnesses. Some witnesses cannot do this, and then we will ask you to intervene from the very beginning. But in most cases, you gave us a memorandum, and through this memorandum, we are now aware of the main reasons why a witness has been asked to come and testify, but, generally, the witness will speak freely about the events he went through. And given the documents that you gave us, pursuant to the Rules, we will see if this witness did not say enough or, on the contrary, if the witness said too much or repeated too many things. Then we will ask you to ask new questions to the witness, but we don't want you to have the witness repeat the same things. We will ask you to ask some questions to the witness so that we can get more clarifications or precisions maybe, because you may think that the witness did not say all the elements that he was supposed to address or to mention in front of this Tribunal. That's the procedure we will be following. As far as the exhibits are concerned, Mr. Registrar, we think that it is appropriate that, in the morning or before trial, both parties give a list of all the exhibits to the Registry. It's much easier. So I think the Prosecution and the Defence should inform the Registry of all the useful exhibits, so that when you need to have one exhibit presented to the witness, this exhibit could be presented to the witness more expeditiously. As far as the exhibits are concerned, and I'm telling this to the technical booth, who are very competent and I do thank them for their work, this exhibit should be presented on the ELMO and on the screens, except when the hearings are closed hearings, but usually we are working in open hearings. And particularly here in this Tribunal, it's very important where international justice is rendered. So when an exhibit is presented to the Judges through the ELMO, this exhibit should also appear on the screens in the courtroom and in the public gallery. These are the main principles I wanted to address. There's one last point, and then I will turn to Mr. Fourmy. I think we should take an order on the contact between witnesses and the parties during the trial, but we will talk about this later so that there is a division between the parties. Of course, it may change in one system or the other, but we're not bound by any national legal system. We want to make sure that the witness, when he is asked to come and testify here, is a witness of justice and not a witness of one of the parties. As soon as the witness enters this courtroom, this witness becomes a witness of justice and should answer primarily to the Judges. The Defence should also know that when some protective measures are asked for, you just have to present a submission, and this could be done in a closed session. This is possible. We started a few moments ago in closed session. Of course, if you want this, the Judges will answer to your submission, and we will go into closed session so that you can present your motions. Are there any other observations? I turn to my colleagues? No? No. Mr. Prosecutor, then I'll give you the floor. Mr. Tochilovsky, shall we start right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, prior to commencing the presentation of the Prosecution's evidence, the Prosecution would like to raise a few issues relevant to the presentation. First, in accordance with Rule 90 of the Rules of Procedure of the ICTY, upon order of the Trial Chamber, an investigator in charge of a party's investigation shall not be precluded from being called as a witness on the ground that he has been present in the courtroom during the proceedings. Subsequently, the Prosecution would request the Trial Chamber to apply this Rule to an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Which paragraph? Which Rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: It is Rule 90, paragraph E. The Prosecution would request the Trial Chamber to apply Rule 90(E) to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecution, Bernard O'Donnell, who is present in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I shall consult with my colleagues. The Judges agree but they wish to note that this provision of the Rules applies to the Defence, as well as to the Prosecution. Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The second issue is the protection of witnesses who are to testify in this portion of our trial, these three days. Upon their arrival to The Hague, the Prosecution witnesses have requested some measures for protection provided for in Rule 75. Subsequently, the Prosecution requests the Trial Chamber to hear the testimony of the Prosecution witnesses in open session in which measures are taken to prevent disclosure to the public or the media of the identity of the victims and witnesses. We discussed the measures with the Defence, and the Defence has no objection to that. The measures that the Prosecution requests for these eight witnesses, in consultation with the Victims and Witnesses Unit, are those provided for in Rule 75(B)(i), namely, such measures as deleting names and identifying information from the Chamber's public records; non-disclosure to the public of any records identifying the witness; giving oral testimony through image-altering devices; assignment of a pseudonym. The written motion for these protective measures is being filed by the Prosecution, but the names of those witnesses who need the protective measures I can give to the Trial Chamber, if we can have a closed session for that. Actually, it's just six witnesses, five of whom would request pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) For these three days, you envisage six witnesses for three days?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, we are calling six witnesses for these three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You wish to submit the motion straightaway? Do you have it in writing? Then we can rule immediately, especially if the Defence has no objection. Mr. Registrar, do you have the motion in writing or has it still not arrived? Then perhaps we can leave it for the afternoon. No? Let's have a private session to agree at least on the measures that we will take for the witness that will be appearing in a couple of minutes, especially if the Defence has no objection. Can we have a private session now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) We will now resume our work. Please be seated. Can the accused be brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) First of all, I will ask the usher to immediately give the headset to the witness. We should know this by now, that the witness needs to have a headset immediately. Can you hear us, Witness? If you can, I will ask you to stand up. I wish your microphone could be switched on. Mr. Usher, could you please switch his microphone on? Thank you. Witness A, can you hear me? Please stand up. Thank you for coming. That's the first thing I would like to say. Please do not say anything right now; first of all, do not tell us what your name is. The usher will hand a sheet of paper to you. On this sheet of paper, you will see your name written down, and you will please tell us "Yes" or "No" whether this is your name. Mr. Usher, could you please hand out this sheet of paper to the witness, please? Witness A, is this your name which appears on this sheet of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. I will ask you to remain standing for a few minutes. The usher will now present you with a solemn declaration which I will ask you to say out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much. You may now be seated. A pseudonym has been attributed to you. You will be Witness A throughout these proceedings. You have come to testify as a Prosecution witness in the case brought by the Prosecutor against Goran Jelisic. Mr. Jelisic has been accused of genocide. You have been granted a number of protective measures. This is the reason why the sound of your voice has been distorted; that is the reason why a pseudonym has been attributed to you. All these measures are part of the regular measures that we grant to witnesses who wish to be protected. We will ask you a number of preliminary questions and then I will ask you to tell us freely what happened to you. It may happen that the Prosecutor will interrupt you and will ask you to give us some more details or to add some elements of information. Then there will be a cross-examination by the Defence counsel and then the Judges will put a few questions to you. Mr. Bowers or Mr. Tochilovsky, is there anything you would like to ask the witness? Do you have any preliminary questions you would like to put to the witness before the witness starts telling us about the events he has been through?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just some questions -- some background information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness A, let me ask you some background information first, and the first question is: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Thirty-seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Witness A, I know this is a very difficult experience for you, I know you must feel very intimidated, but you have to speak out for the interpreters. The interpreters cannot hear you if you do not speak directly in the microphone. They need to hear what you are saying because we need to have your testimony interpreted into the official languages of this Tribunal. If you don't feel at ease, please say so, and we will suspend the hearing. At any rate, we won't go beyond 6.00, but if anything should happen and if you don't feel at ease at any particular moment, please say so. Mr. Tochilovsky, did you ask for the voice of the witness to be distorted or did you only ask for his face to be distorted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Only the face.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: The last question, which is relevant to the background information is: Where did you live before the war, Witness A?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you would allow me, I would start with general questions relevant to this case and then we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Of course, Mr. Tochilovsky. We all have to get used to the different principles I set out before the break. The essential thing is for you to try and launch the witness in his testimony and then let him speak freely. Afterwards, maybe you will feel the need to ask some more questions, but first of all, let's try to have the witness start his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness A, were you detained in Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, when did you arrive to Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened upon your arrival to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I do not quite understand. Do you mean -- shall I describe it, the arrival itself or what went on after I arrived?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell the Court what happened immediately upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Immediately upon our arrival, we were lined up against a wall of the hangar. The soldier who had brought us there, who was put in charge of our -- I don't know how to put it. I don't know how to express myself -- who was responsible for us, who was put in charge to bring us to the Luka camp, he addressed the other soldiers and said, "Here, I brought some more balijas." And the soldiers who were there were Serbian soldiers, to put it that way, but they themselves called each other Chetniks and so did we. They started beating us and verbally abusing us. They called us "Gang," they said "We'll kill you all. Nobody's going to save you."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness A, you mentioned that the soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can we have the second microphone also turned on, please, in front of the witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: These were the guards in the camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? The question is: When you arrived, you just said that they called you balijas. Is "balija" a derogatory name for Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me just ask you, how do you want me to describe it? I would have to go into a lengthier explanation to tell you what "balija" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Please feel free to express yourself. Please tell us what happened once you entered the camp, why were you brought to the camp, and tell us what happened inside the camp. If the Prosecutor feels the need to have more details, then he will ask you to provide us these details, but the essential thing for us is not to have you repeat anything. We don't want you to have to go over these events again and again. But, please, express yourself quite freely, Witness A.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: If I could have the assistance of the usher, Mr. President, in placing Prosecutor's Exhibit 341 in front of the witness and distributing it to counsel and the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) We do seem to have a small technical problem. You see, Witness A, there is a problem with your voice. We have implemented the voice distortion device which means that the interpreters can't hear you very clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Exhibit number 2. Exhibit number 1 being the sheet of paper which was shown to the witness earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness A, does the photo depict the hangar in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to indicate certain locations on the photo which are relevant to your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Is the location marked as X-2 the place where you were lined up upon your arrival to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was Goran Jelisic among those soldiers who were at the hangar when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Goran Jelisic was not in front of the hangar when we arrived there. He arrived five minutes later after one of the soldiers had called him from the office which he shared with Ivan Repic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he was the director of the collection centre and that we had been brought here, that we would be interrogated, and who would be found guilty would be killed and who was going to be found not guilty would be released, and in his words, he said that he did not believe that there was a single balija who was not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic introduce himself after that first day on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, there was a mistake. He said there was not a single "body" who was not guilty or a single "balija" was not guilty, in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court, did you mention "balija" or "body"? Could you explain to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: He used those words, and what he meant to say was that all balijas were guilty, they should all disappear, that they should all die, that they should all be eradicated, and "balija" was for "Muslims"; in other words, he was saying that all the Muslims were guilty, that this nation did not exist, that we have been invented, that we descended from the Turks. So that was the meaning of it, that the Muslims were guilty for the simple fact of being alive. So that was his belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Did Goran Jelisic introduce himself on other occasions and did he call himself by any other name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Now, I cannot recall whether this was the very same day or the next day. He came to the hangar where we had been put because after our group, additional people arrived, and he addressed the people who were at the front of the hangar, he told them that his name was Goran Jelisic, that he was also called Adolf, that he was in command of the group which blew up the bridge over the Sava River, and on this bridge, about 100 people were killed during that explosion, men, women, and children, even small babies. This is the assessment of the police sources. He said that he had killed about 150 people in the Luka camp and that it wasn't all, that he was going to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: With regard to Goran Jelisic, have you seen his picture in any media after you left the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise him if you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Well, even though more than six years have gone by and many things have changed, including my life after the camp, I still believe that I would recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you see Goran Jelisic in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I would like to request of Their Honours if Mr. Jelisic could get up and turn up his sleeves. Can he turn them around because he should have a big scar on his arm, for which he claimed that he got it in Croatia. I cannot see it well from here, but he did have this scar which he claimed to have received in Croatia in a camp. And later, I heard from others, other camp inmates, in the Luka camp that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Excuse me. I want to confer with my colleagues. Mr. Prosecutor, could you approach the bench, please, and also Mr. Londrovic as well, could he approach the bench? Please sit down, Mr. Jelisic, for the time being. Mr. Londrovic, will you approach the bench? Mr. Greaves as well, please. The Judges are going to ask Witness A why this scar was on the arm which would have enabled you to recognise the accused. Why did he have this scar? Could you tell the Judges?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Because he would show that scar to all of us in the hangar, and he tried to tell us a story, according to which he too was detained in a Croatian camp because he had been a volunteer in the Croatian theatre of war and that the Croats had poured salt on his wounds made with a knife to make them more painful. And he boasted of that scar, and I saw that scar, not just I, but all the others who were in the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Thank you, Witness A. You may continue. Yes, Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Witness A, did you have a good view? Do you see well? Is your vision good? Do you see well at a distance? Can you recognise people at a distance or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: People that I see on a daily basis or who I saw a year ago, I would recognise certainly, but I haven't seen him for more than six years, and he has changed also. He's not the same person he was six years ago physically, though some features still remain, but it is not the same face that it was six years ago. He has calmed down -- he has changed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: -- just as I have changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well, Mr. Tochilovsky, please proceed with your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Was Goran Jelisic wearing any uniform on him at that time when you were in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: With regard to that scar, you just explained that Goran Jelisic represented it as a scar as a result of his detention in Croatia. Do you know another explanation for that scar? Have you heard about any other explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes. I heard from others, other detainees in the Luka camp, because he had given a different story to some others. He personally, according to this other story, he had been wounded when he was interrogating or, rather, when he wanted to kill Fritz, and "Fritz" is the nickname of a commercial inspector in the municipality. His surname is Novalic. The person is deceased. He was killed by Jelisic. According to Jelisic's statement and the statements of other witnesses that I heard, he tried to attack Jelisic with an axe to defend himself because this one wanted to kill him, and eventually, he, in fact, did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness A, can you describe what happened on that first night in the Luka camp with you and the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: After the mistreatment initially in front of the hangar when we were brought in, this went on, I couldn't tell you exactly for how long, because when one is fearful, things last an eternity, and one only thinks about reducing the pain from each blow as much as possible and avoiding the blow and just to keep alive. That is the only thought in his mind. So afterwards, under blows, we were pushed into the front part of the hangar, and we were ordered to sit down on the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: And what happened to you and the other detainees at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: We stayed like that, sitting there all day until the evening. Roughly, it might have been about 8.00, 7.30, the door of the hangar through which we had come in was closed, and outside, singing could be heard, their Chetnik songs, provocations to the effect, "Balija, you've had it. There's a little left for you. We will exterminate you," and things like that. Then music could be heard from a tape recorder. And during the night -- no one could have known the exact time because all our watches and valuables, rings, everything we had had been seized from us, even our personal documents. Anyway, it was before midnight. The door was opened but not altogether, just enough to allow a person to pass through without hitting the door frame or the door walking out, and they called for four volunteers to do a job. We didn't know at all that, besides us, there were others in the camp, in the hangar. The part of the hangar where we were, in the middle, there was another door leading to another part of the hangar. As it was dark and the door was more or less closed, we couldn't see whether there were any people in the other part of the hangar, and only once the door was opened and when people started coming out did we see that we were not alone there, that, in addition to us, there were others. Four men came out of the other part through the door, and one could hear blows outside, that these four volunteers were being beaten outside, that they were called balijas, the Turkish gang. They cursed their Muslim mothers. I couldn't see anything, but I could hear all of this. People were moaning, begging, "Don't do that. We are not guilty of anything." To the background of these moans and blows and all of this, a voice could be heard, a voice that I recognised later on because I heard it every day, the order was, "Lie down. Lean your head against the grate." Then, "Don't. Don't do that to me. Why me? I haven't done anything. I'm not guilty." Again, moans of the same man, most probably, because I couldn't see anything. This was all to no avail. One could just hear a silenced shot, and very briefly after that, like a vibration of the concrete, because there was just one wall separating me from the spot where the people were killed. After that, maybe two or three minutes later, then the same sound, the shot, a silenced shot, then the blunt sound of a blow against the concrete, preceded, of course, by blows, by screams, by moans, "Don't do that. Why? I've always lived with the Serbs here in peace. I haven't done anything. I never hurt any Serbs." But all of this was to no avail. I'm saying this in this way because I didn't see anything through the wall. But I'm saying this precisely because I too was a volunteer on two occasions. I went outside and I saw with my own eyes how people were mistreated, beaten --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, Witness A? With regard to the fact when you volunteered, when you went out, can you provide some more details about the incidents you saw when you went out, and please refer to the photo that you have, Exhibit 2, where you were staying and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I went out as one of four volunteers on the second or third day; I can't remember exactly. Before me, there were about ten groups of four volunteers each. People were afraid to go out. They knew what to expect. And then they started yelling from the door, "Come out, balijas, come out. Don't let us come in and select those who will go out." Considering the fear I had been in, particularly after May the 3rd when I was mistreated by the Chetniks, I simply didn't care anymore. I went out to put an end to all this suffering, and I thought it was all the same to me, whether it happened today or tomorrow, because it appeared that the same fate would befall all of us. So I went out, and as soon as I got out, they started hitting, cursing, shouting, "Balijas, there's no salvation for you," curses, Muslim mothers were cursed, and everything else that they could think of. They lined us up here (indicating), they forced us to line up against the wall with our heads bent down, our hands behind our backs --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you referring to location X-1 for the record?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes, yes, X-1, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: What happened next after you were taken out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: I was the third in line, counting from this end, the end of the hangar or the beginning of the hangar. There were two men in front of me, then I, then another one after me. The second man in our group was approached by Ivan, known as Repic. The other soldiers moved away from us, they stopped beating us, and he pulled this man out of the group and ordered him to lie down on the asphalt and to put his head on this grate marked as X-3. The man pleaded, "Don't. Let me go." The same words were used by all. Everyone wanted to live. Nobody wanted to be killed. But that didn't help. Whether the victim put his head down of his own free will or was forced to do so by them, it was the same for them so long as they killed him. What is more, it was my impression that they enjoyed it more when the victim pleaded with them. The more the victim pleaded not to be killed, to be allowed to live, the more they enjoyed the killing. Also, the first time that I went out in a group, Jelisic was doing the killing. The second time, it was Miroslav. My impression was and still is that they really enjoyed the killing of helpless people. Many times I asked myself whether those beasts in human form, if I could call them that, would they have the courage in the street to fight one on one and to look us in the face, and how would they behave then? But like this, to treat unarmed, helpless captives, 20-to-1, in those conditions, they were very brave and they enjoyed what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes? You have another question? Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Witness A, after Goran Jelisic killed the person, did he order you to carry the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Can you explain, where did you carry the bodies? Were you told where to carry the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: They told me and the first man, the one who was first in line while the group was still whole, and under blows they forced us to carry the dead body, to carry it. I carried the man by his arms, the other one by his legs, and we carried him to here (indicating), the corner here, the edge of the building, and behind it, a truck was parked, a refrigerator lorry. We only saw the back flap open, it was dark, and in the dark, we reached the truck, we threw in the body, and in doing so, I saw that there were other bodies in the lorry. We came back, again under blows and insults. "The same fate awaits you," they said. We formed a group again, which now, unfortunately, consisted of only three men. I was the first now in the group, because while they were beating us on the way back, the man in front of me ran off, and I followed him, so that he stood next to the other man and I next to this one. We didn't stand at attention for long when a man was brought out again, the same man that had carried the first body with me, and he was killed in the same way as the first man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Who killed the man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A
utterances.text: The first and the second man were killed by Goran Jelisic, and while doing so, he said, "Another balija less." After that, I and the last remaining man in the group were forced once again to carry the body to the truck, to throw it in, into the truck, and then we returned, again under blows. This time we thought it would be our turn, but they continued beating us and forcing us in the direction of the door of the hangar, saying, "Get in, balijas, and get ready, because in a day or two, it will be your turn." Not long afterwards, maybe ten or fifteen minutes later, maybe even less, because minutes appeared like hours to us, hours like years, the next group of volunteers was called out, and so it went on until morning, 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning. At the end, in the night, a group of seven or eight men would be called out who had to clean the blood which could be seen everywhere, around the grate and on the grate rails itself, to remove all traces of their savagery and their crimes. This was repeated every night. It went on until the early hours of the morning until the day when Goran Jelisic entered the hangar with Major Dzurkovic and a captain who was wearing a uniform of the former Yugoslav People's Army, as was the major, Major Dzurkovic, accompanied by several guards, and then they read out -- or, rather, they didn't read out, they just told us, that killing was prohibited, killing and mistreatment of prisoners, of detainees. The men started to applaud. Some even raised him onto their shoulders, which hurt me so much. In that moment, I couldn't really accept that after everything this beast had done, that men could have raised him up on their shoulders. I couldn't applaud him, never mind lift him up. I would have rather dropped dead than do that. But I later had more understanding for those men because the words he had spoken, the order which had come from someone up there, someone from their leadership, meant that we were born again, that we could continue to live, that we had survived, unlike our other compatriots. After that - was it that day or the next day? - a guard came into the hangar with a big notebook in his hands and a pen and ordered us to line up, and he wrote down our names one by one, our first and last names, date of birth, addresses, where we used to live, because our address at the time they were taking it down was the Luka camp. Only then did we become human beings with names and surnames, with former addresses, and a new address, the Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Excuse me. May I interrupt you, Witness A? If I can continue? I just have a few questions for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No. You know, it is a quarter past 6.00. This witness -- first of all, we had planned to adjourn at 6.00. Even though the witness has not been testifying for long, he's re-experiencing all that very emotionally. We will meet again tomorrow at 10.00. Try, I can't say to forget, but to relax a little, and I hope the Witnesses and Victims Unit will take care of the witness. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: So we can continue tomorrow with this Witness A?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am saying that he will be taken care of by the Victims and Witnesses Unit. He won't be alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, this Victims and Witnesses Unit takes care of our witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. We will now adjourn and resume tomorrow morning at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.16 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of December, 1998, at 10.00 a.m.
